title: Alaska seeks dismissal of DOJ lawsuit over Senate ballot certification - Whatfinger News Quick Hits
text:
Alaska’s Republican-led government asked a federal court to dismiss a Justice Department lawsuit aimed at blocking certification of the state’s Senate election results over same-name ballot concerns.
Attorneys for Alaska and other defendants filed the motion Monday, telling a federal judge the Department of Justice has no legal basis to stop the state from certifying its midterm results in the U.S. Senate race.
The fight centers on two candidates named Sullivan. Incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican, is on the ballot opposite Democrat Mary Peltola. Another Republican, Daniel J. Sullivan, also entered the race, prompting the Justice Department to sue last week and seek a bar on certification.
The Hill reported that President Trump said he directed the Justice Department to file the case. Alaska’s filing pushes back hard on federal power and on the claim that voters cannot tell the candidates apart.
State lawyers argued the elections division already separated the names on the ballot. They said the complaint itself fails.
“has taken significant steps to distinguish them on the ballot so that voters can easily determine which candidate is which.”
The motion went further on federal authority. Attorneys for Alaska and the other defendants wrote that Washington has no business inserting itself into the state’s election process.
“the United States lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate,”
They added a blunt bottom line: “the complaint has no legal basis.”
That posture tracks a broader pattern of states resisting federal election interventions, including earlier coverage of how the DOJ moved against Alaska certification over the second Sullivan on the ballot.
The Justice Department’s own filing painted a different picture. It claimed Daniel J. Sullivan entered the race “with the intention of misleading” supporters of the incumbent. The department warned that certifying results with him on the ballot would breach the state’s duty to protect election integrity.
“Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan… the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election,”
DOJ lawyers argued the same-name pairing could hand Peltola an unfair edge. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department was not trying to halt certification outright. He framed the suit as a preservation step so Alaska’s own officials could later decide whether voters were confused or misled.
“to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska’s governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or mislead.”
Ballot design details attached to the state’s filing undercut the confusion claim. The sample shows the word “incumbent” next to the sitting senator’s name, along with party affiliation. Middle initials also differ: the incumbent appears as “Sullivan, Dan S.” The other candidate is listed as “Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.” The design does not note the second Sullivan’s registered Republican status in the same way.
Those distinctions matter in a race already marked by name overlap, a point underscored when a former Anchorage mayor backed Sen. Dan Sullivan and addressed the same ballot confusion directly.
Peltola’s campaign joined the push to kill the federal suit. Her lawyers asked the court to dismiss the Justice Department’s case and called it “wholly baseless.”
Common Cause, a nonprofit watchdog represented by ACLU attorneys, filed a motion last week to intervene in the litigation. U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason ordered expedited handling on Monday and gave the federal government until 5 p.m. Tuesday to respond to both the Peltola campaign’s motion and Common Cause’s request.
The compressed schedule puts the dispute on a fast track while ballots and certification timelines loom. Similar urgency has marked other Justice Department election fights this cycle, including cases where courts set tight deadlines as the DOJ pressed ballot sequestration steps in California.
At its core, the Alaska case collides two principles conservatives usually defend at once: clean elections and limits on federal power. The Justice Department says a second Sullivan risks misleading voters and skewing a Senate contest. Alaska’s Republican-led government says the state already labeled the ballot clearly, and that the United States has no warrant to dictate certification or pick favorites.
Trump’s decision to direct the filing places the administration squarely behind the integrity argument. Alaska’s motion answers that the proper guardians of the ballot are the state’s own officers, not lawyers from Washington. Democrats, meanwhile, have been building legal capacity for these fights, as seen when Democratic teams geared up against DOJ election challenges across multiple states.
The Senate race itself sits inside a larger Alaska election-system debate. Trump has already urged voters there to reject ranked-choice voting, calling it a Democratic scam in prior remarks that framed Alaska’s voting rules as tilted against straightforward majorities.
None of the filings released in the initial reports resolve how many voters, if any, mixed up the two Sullivans. The state points to incumbent tags, party labels, and middle initials. The Justice Department points to the shared surname and alleged intent to confuse. Judge Gleason’s expedited order means the legal arguments will land quickly. Certification still belongs, under Alaska’s theory, to Alaska.
Federal lawsuits over state ballots test more than one candidate’s name. They test who runs elections in this country, and whether Washington can freeze a state’s results when it dislikes the lineup on the page.
States that run clean, clearly marked elections should not need permission from the Justice Department to certify them.
